text: Application of Newton's Laws. Solving Newton's Laws. Note, this chapter combines several tools developed earlier in the course. We use vector components from chapter 2, acceleration vectors from chapter 4, and free body diagrams from chapter 5 to apply Newton's second law to real systems. Problem-solving strategies. Applying Newton's Laws of Motion. Most problems in this chapter follow the same pattern. Choose a system, identify the external forces, turn those forces into components, and apply Newton's second law. Define the system of interest. Decide which object or group of objects you are analyzing. Newton's second law uses only the external forces acting on that system. Choose useful axes. Pick coordinate axes that make the force components as simple as possible. When motion occurs along a slope, curve, or rope, it is often useful to align one axis with the motion or acceleration. Draw a free body diagram. Draw only the external forces acting on the chosen system. Do not draw velocity, acceleration, or the net force as separate forces. Write Newton's second law by components. Start from some vector f equals m vector a. Then write the component equations such as some f sub x equals m a sub x, and some f sub y equals m a sub y. Use constraints and known conditions. Constant velocity means a equals zero. Static equilibrium means the net force is zero. A massless rope has the same tension throughout. A frictionless pulley changes the direction of the tension, but not its magnitude. Solve symbolically before evaluating. Keep the algebra general as long as possible. Substitute numerical values only after the physical relationships are clear. Check the result. The answer should have the correct units, the correct direction, and a physically reasonable size. This strategy is not a recipe for memorizing equations. It is a way to translate a physical situation into Newton's second law. The hardest step is usually deciding what belongs in the free body diagram and what does not. See the flipping physics video on the course webpage. Consider the challenge of lifting a grand piano into a second story apartment, which of Newton's laws are involved. Figure shows that we can represent all forces with arrows and simplify the analysis with a more crude representation. It is important to make a list of knowns and unknowns so that we can properly identify the system of interest. Recall that Newton's second law involves only external forces. So we first list all the forces and then identify which are internal or external. The identified forces are vector T, tension in the rope above the piano, vector F sub T, force that the piano exerts on the rope, and vector W, weight of the piano. All other forces, for example the nudge of a breeze, are assumed to be negligible. Newton's third law can be used to identify whether forces are exerted between internal components of a system, or between the system and an external component. The vector T and vector F sub T form a force pair, where we only include the external component vector T in our free body diagram. See Figure B. Figure C shows a free body diagram where Newton's second law is applied in figure D. Once external forces are clearly identified in free body diagrams, it should be straightforward to put them into Newton's second law and form equations that can be solved. If the problem is one-dimensional, i.e. forces or parallel, then the forces can be handled algebraically. If the problem is two-dimensional, then it must be broken into components and then solved as a pair of one-dimensional problems. It is usually convenient to make one-axis parallel to the direction of motion, if this is known. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. Which forces act on the chosen system, and which forces act on something outside the system? Then you have some F sub X equals M A sub X. Some F sub Y equals M A sub Y. We must check the solution to tell whether it is reasonable. For example, it is reasonable to find that friction causes an object to slide down an incline more slowly than when no friction exists. In practice, intuition, i.e. knowing what is reasonable at a glance, develops through solving many problems, i.e. experience. Ut est rarem amniam magister usus. Experience is the teacher of all things, Julius Caesar. Another way to check a solution is to check the units. If we are solving for force and end up with units of only velocity, then we have made a mistake. Particle equilibrium. A particle in equilibrium is one that obeys Newton's first law, i.e. the external forces are balanced. Static equilibrium involves objects at rest, and dynamic equilibrium involves objects in motion without acceleration. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If an object is moving at constant velocity, is it an equilibrium? What does that imply about the sum vector F? Particle equilibrium is the force version of constant velocity. If the acceleration is zero, Newton's second law becomes sum vector F equals zero. This extends the equilibrium ideas from Newton's first law and the free body diagram workflow from chapter 5. Example problem. Different tensions at different angles. The problem. Consider the traffic light, mass of 15 kilograms, suspended from two wires as shown in figure. Find the tension in each wire, neglecting the masses of the wires. The worked solution follows. The model. The system of interest is the traffic light. We model the traffic light as a particle in static equilibrium, so its acceleration is zero. We choose plus i hat to point horizontally to the right and plus j hat to point vertically upward. With this coordinate choice, the left wire tension vector T sub 1 points up and to the left. The right wire tension vector T sub 2 points up and to the right, and the weight vector W points downward in the negative j hat direction. The left wire makes an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal, and the right wire makes an angle of 45 degrees with the horizontal. The two wires are treated as massless and inexpensive, so each wire exerts a tension force along its own direction. The only forces acting on the traffic light are the two tensions and the weight, similar to the tension in a tight rope. Air resistance and motion of the light are neglected. The math. For static equilibrium, Newton's second law requires the net force on the traffic light to be zero. Since the traffic light has no acceleration in either direction, some f sub x equals m a sub x equals zero. Some f sub y equals m a sub y equals zero. The forces acting on the traffic light are the left tension vector T sub 1, the right tension vector T sub 2, and the weight vector W equals negative mg j hat. Resolving the two tension forces into horizontal and vertical components gives the component equations. Some f sub x equals negative T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals zero. Some f sub y equals T sub 1 sine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 sine 45 degrees minus mg equals zero. The horizontal equation relates the two unknown tensions. We solve this equation for T sub 2 in terms of T sub 1 so that the vertical equation will contain only one unknown tension. Negative T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals zero. T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees. The vertical equation determines the actual size of the tensions because the vertical components must balance the weight of the traffic light. We substitute the horizontal equilibrium relation for T sub 2 into the vertical equation and solve for T sub 1. T sub 1 sign 30 degrees plus T sub 2 sign 45 degrees minus mg equals 0. T sub 1 sign 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sign 45 degrees equals mg. T sub 1 times sign 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sign 45 degrees equals mg. T sub 1 equals mg over sine 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sine 45 degrees. The numerical value of T sub 1 follows from the vertical force balance, and then the horizontal force balance gives T sub 2. T sub 1 equals 15.0 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared over sine 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sine 45 degrees equals 108 newtons. T sub 2 equals T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees equals 108 newtons times cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees equals 132 newtons. The conclusion, the tension in the left wire is T sub 1 equals 108 newtons, and the tension in the right wire is T sub 2 equals 132 newtons. The right wire has the larger tension because its direction is closer to vertical, so it supplies more of the upward force needed to balance the traffic light's weight. These values satisfy newtons' second law for static equilibrium because the horizontal components cancel and the vertical components balance the weight. Particle acceleration. Instead of reducing the problem to a particle in static equilibrium where the sum of the net forces equals 0, we can also reduce complex problems into one where the net force is non-zero, or a particle with an acceleration. When the net force is not 0, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force. The vector equation, the sum of the force vectors equals mass times the acceleration vector, is solved component by component using the same vector component ideas introduced in chapter 2. We'll look through four examples that illustrate different ways we can decompose the complex motion into a simpler one. Drag force on a barge, net force in an elevator, two attached blocks connected with a pulley, and at-wood machine vertical blocks with a pulley. Note, it is useful to identify constraints that make a problem solvable. We saw this in the tension in a tight-rope problem when identifying the tension. In chapter 5, we showed that the normal force, a contact force, acts normal to the surface so that an object does not have an acceleration perpendicular to the surface, meaning it stays static. The bathroom scale is an excellent example of a normal force acting on a body. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If the acceleration is 0 in one direction, but non-zero in another, which component equations of Newton's second law still matter? A bathroom scale provides a measure of how much it must push upward to support the weight of an object. The net force in an elevator problem will examine whether we can predict what you would measure on a bathroom scale that is moving upward, either accelerating or moving at constant speed. Do you think the scale will measure a different weight when the elevator is moving at constant speed? What if the elevator is accelerating upward? Take a guess before looking at the example problem. Example problem. Drag force on a barge. The problem. Two tugboats push on a barge at different angles as shown in figure. The first tugboat exerts a force of 2.7 times 10 to the fifth Newton's in the x direction, and the second tugboat exerts a force of 3.6 times 10 to the fifth Newton's in the y direction. The mass of the barge is 5 times 10 to the sixth kilograms, and its acceleration is observed to be 7.5 times 10 to the minus 2 meters per second squared in the direction shown. What is the drag force of the water on the barge resisting the motion? Note. Drag force is a frictional force exerted by fluids such as air or water. The drag force opposes the motion of the object. Since the barge is flat bottomed, we can assume that the drag force is in the direction opposite the barge's motion. The worked solution follows. The model. The system of interest is the barge. We model the barge as a rigid object translating on the horizontal surface of the water. We choose plus i hat to point in the direction of the first tugboats force, and plus j hat to point in the direction of the second tugboats force. With this coordinate choice, the tugboat forces are vector f sub 1 equals f sub 1 i hat, and vector f sub 2 equals f sub 2 j hat. The resultant tugboat force vector f sub app points in the direction of the barge's observed acceleration. The drag force exerted by the water points opposite the barge's motion, so it points opposite vector f sub app. The weight of the barge and the buoyant force from the water balance vertically, so they are omitted from the horizontal force model. The math. For horizontal motion, Newton's second law relates the net horizontal force on the barge to the observed acceleration of the barge. The forces acting on the barge in the horizontal plane are the tugboat forces vector f sub 1 and vector f sub 2, and the drag force vector f sub d. The two tugboat forces combine to form the applied force vector vector f sub app, and the drag force acts opposite the barge's motion. Newton's second law for the horizontal motion is some vector f equals m vector a. Vector f sub app plus vector f sub d equals m vector a. The two tugboat forces are perpendicular, so the magnitude and direction of the applied force come from the vector components of vector f sub app. Resolving the applied force into components gives vector f sub app equals f sub 1 i hat plus f sub 2 j hat. f app equals square root of f sub 1 to the power of 2 plus f sub 2 to the power of 2. Theta equals 10 to the power of minus 1 f sub 2 over f sub 1. The applied force magnitude and direction follow from the perpendicular tugboat force components by f app equals square root of 2.7 times 10 to the 5 newtons squared plus 3.6 times 10 to the 5 newtons squared equals 4.5 times 10 to the 5 newtons. Theta equals 10 to the power of negative 1, 3.6 times 10 to the 5 over 2.7 times 10 to the 5 equals 53 degrees. Along the direction of motion the applied force points forward and the drag force points backward. Newton's second law along this direction gives f app minus f sub d equals ma. We solve this equation for the drag force magnitude which yields f sub d equals f app minus ma. The drag force follows from Newton's second law along the direction of motion as f sub d equals 4.5 times 10 to the 5 newtons minus 5 times 10 to the sixth kilograms times 7.5 times 10 to the minus 2 meters per second squared equals 7.5 times 10 to the 4th newtons. The conclusion the water exerts a drag force with magnitude f sub d equals 7.5 times 10 to the 4th newtons. This drag force acts opposite the barge's motion while the tugboat resultant points in the direction of motion. The result is consistent with Newton's second law because the applied tugboat force is larger than the drag force leaving a net force that accelerates the barge. Example problem, bathroom scale in an elevator. The problem, the figure on the course web page shows a 75 kilogram man weight of about 165 pounds standing on a bathroom scale in an elevator. Calculate the scale reading. A, if the elevator accelerates upward at a rate of 1.2 meters per second squared, and B, if the elevator moves upward at a constant speed of 1 meter per second. The worked solution follows. The model. The system of interest is the person standing on the scale. We model the person as a particle moving vertically with the elevator. We choose plus j hat to point upward and minus j hat to point downward. With this coordinate choice, the scale force on the person points upward, so vector f sub s equals f sub s j hat, and the weight of the person points downward, so vector w equals minus mg j hat. The scale reading is the magnitude of the upward contact force f sub s. Air resistance is neglected, and the motion is one-dimensional along the vertical axis. The math. For vertical motion, Newton's second law relates the net vertical force on the person to the person's vertical acceleration. The forces acting on the person are the upward scale force vector f sub s, and the downward weight vector w. Applying Newton's second law in the vertical direction gives some f sub y equals m a sub y. f sub s minus mg equals m a sub y. We solve this equation for the scale reading, f sub s, which yields f sub s equals mg plus m a sub y. f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y. This equation shows that the scale reading depends on the vertical acceleration of the person. A. First, we evaluate the case when the elevator accelerates upward at a sub y equals 1.20 meters per second squared. Since the acceleration points in the plus j hat direction, a sub y is positive. f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y equals 75.0 kilograms times the quantity 9.81 meters per second squared plus 1.20 meters per second squared equals 826 newtons. B. Then we evaluate the case when the elevator moves upward at a constant speed of 1 meter per second. Constance speed implies a sub y equals 0. So f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y equals 75.0 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared plus 0 equals 736 newtons. The conclusion. When the elevator accelerates upward at 1.20 meters per second squared, the scale reads f sub s equals 826 newtons. When the elevator moves upward at constant speed, the acceleration is 0, and the scale reads f sub s equals 736 newtons. The scale reading is larger during upward acceleration because the scale must exert enough upward force to both balance the person's weight and produce the upward acceleration. Example problem. Two attached blocks. The problem. The figure on the course web page shows a block of mass m sub 1 on a frictionless horizontal surface. It is pulled by a light string that passes over a frictionless and massless pulley. The other end of the string is connected to a block of mass m sub 2. Find the acceleration of the blocks and the tension in the string in terms of m sub 1, m sub 2, and g. The worked solution follows. The model. The system consists of two blocks connected by a light inextensible string over a frictionless, massless pulley. Block m sub 1 moves horizontally on a frictionless table and block m sub 2 moves vertically. The string constrains the blocks to have the same acceleration magnitude. For block m sub 1, we choose plus i hat to point to the right and plus j hat to point upward. With this convention, the tension vector t points in the plus i hat direction. The normal force vector n points in the plus j hat direction and the weight vector w sub 1 points in the negative j hat direction. For block m sub 2, we use plus j hat upward, so the tension vector t points in the plus j hat direction and the weight vector w sub 2 points in the negative j hat direction. The hanging block accelerates downward while the block on the table accelerates to the right. This example uses the same free body diagram workflow developed in chapter 5. The important step here is to apply Newton's second law separately to each block and then use the string constraint to relate their accelerations. The math. For the connected block system, Newton's second law must be applied separately to each block because the tension is an internal interaction between the two blocks. The forces acting on block m sub 1 are the tension, the normal force, and its weight. The vertical forces on m sub 1 balance while the horizontal tension provides its acceleration to the right. Applying Newton's second law to block m sub 1 gives some f sub 1 x equals m sub 1 a t equals m sub 1 a. The forces acting on block m sub 2 are the upward tension and the downward weight. Since plus j hat points upward, but m sub 2 accelerates downward, its vertical acceleration is a sub 2 y equals minus a. Applying Newton's second law to block m sub 2 gives some f sub 2 y equals m sub 2 a sub 2 y t minus m sub 2 g equals minus m sub 2 a. These two equations form the governing equations for the system t equals m sub 1 a t minus m sub 2 g equals minus m sub 2 a. We solve these equations for the acceleration by substituting t equals m sub 1 a into the equation for block m sub 2. m sub 1 a minus m sub 2 g equals minus m sub 2 a m sub 1 a plus m sub 2 a equals m sub 2 g m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times a equals m sub 2 g a equals m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g. We then use the block m sub 1 equation to solve for the tension t equals m sub 1 a t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g. The conclusion, the two blocks accelerate with magnitude a equals m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g. Block m sub 1 accelerates to the right and block m sub 2 accelerates downward. The tension in the string is t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 g. The acceleration is less than g because the weight of the hanging block must accelerate both masses, not just m sub 2. Example problem, at-wood machine. The problem, a classic problem in physics, similar to the one we just solved, is the at-wood machine, which consists of a light rope running over a frictionless pulley with two objects of different mass attached. It is particularly useful in understanding the connection between force and motion. In figure, the masses are m sub 1 equals 2 kilograms and m sub 2 equals 4 kilograms. The pulley is frictionless. A, if m sub 2 is released, what will its acceleration be? B, what is the tension in the string? The worked solution follows. The model. Each mass is modeled as a particle connected by a light, inextensible string over a frictionless, massless pulley. The ideal string and pulley make the tension magnitude the same on both sides of the pulley. The string constraint makes the blocks have the same acceleration magnitude. We choose plus j hat to point upward for both blocks. With this convention, the tension on block m sub 1, points in the plus j hat direction and the weight of block m sub 1 points in the minus j hat direction. The tension on block m sub 2 also points in the plus j hat direction and the weight of block m sub 2 points in the minus j at direction. Since m sub 2 is greater than m sub 1, block m sub 2 accelerates downward and block M sub 1 accelerates upward. This problem is closely related to the previous attached blocks example. In both problems, Newton's second law is applied separately to each block, and the string constraint connects their accelerations. The math. For the at-wood machine, Newton's second law must be applied separately to each block, because the tension is an internal interaction between the two masses. The forces acting on block M sub 1 are the upward tension and the downward weight. Since block M sub 1 accelerates upward in the plus j hat direction, Newton's second law gives some F sub 1 y equals M sub 1 A. T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A. The forces acting on block M sub 2 are also the upward tension and the downward weight. Since block M sub 2 accelerates downward while plus j hat points upward, its acceleration is minus A j hat. Newton's second law gives some F sub 2 y equals M sub 2 times minus A. T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A. These two equations form the governing equations for the system and will be reused in both parts. T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A. T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A. A. First, we determine the acceleration of the blocks after M sub 2 is released. We eliminate the tension by subtracting the equation for block M sub 1 from the equation for block M sub 2 and then solve for A. T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A minus M sub 1 A. M sub 1 minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 1 plus M sub 2 A. In turn, A equals M sub 2 minus M sub 1 over M sub 1 plus M sub 2 G. The acceleration follows from the mass difference and the total mass being accelerated. A equals 4.00 kilograms minus 2.00 kilograms over 4.00 kilograms plus 2.00 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared equals 3.27 meters per second squared. B. Next, we find the tension in the string by reusing the equation for block M sub 1. We solve that equation for T and substitute the acceleration found in part A. T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A. T equals M sub 1 times G plus A. T equals 2.00 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared plus 3.27 meters per second squared equals 26.2 newtons. The conclusion. The blocks accelerate with magnitude A equals 3.27 meters per second squared. Block M sub 2 accelerates downward and block M sub 1 accelerates upward. The tension in the string is T equals 26.2 newtons. This result closely mirrors the attached blocks problem. The acceleration is determined by the net unbalanced weight divided by the total mass being accelerated. Newton's laws of motion and kinematics. Newton's laws of motion can also be integrated with other concepts to solve problems of motion. For example, forces produce accelerations, which was the main topic when discussing kinematics. Newton's second law gives the acceleration. Once the acceleration is known, the motion is found using the kinematics tools developed earlier, including constant acceleration motion in chapter 3 and vector motion in chapter 4. For problems that involve various types of forces, acceleration, velocity, or position, it helps to identify the principles involved when listing the givens and quantities to be calculated. The following examples illustrate how to apply the problem solving strategies. These example problems are soccer player at top speed, force on a model helicopter, force on a baggage tractor, and the motion of a vertical projectile as a bonus. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. When a force determines acceleration first, which kinematics quantities should you compute next, velocity, position, or time? Recall that V equals DS over DT and A equals DV over DT. This means that we can use the calculus forms when acceleration is not constant, meaning A equals a function of S, V, and T. First, we solve for DT in each equation, then set them equal to each other. DT equals DS divided by V, DT equals DV divided by A. So, A DS equals V DV. When A is a function of V, we can apply the following integrals. A of V times the integral of DS equals the integral of V DV, and the integral of DS equals the integral of V divided by A of V with respect to V. Example problem. Soccer player top speed. The problem. A soccer player starts at rest and accelerates forward reaching a velocity of 8 meters per second in 2.5 seconds. A, what is her average acceleration? B, what average force does the ground exert forward on the runner so that she achieves this acceleration? The player's mass is 70 kilograms and air resistance is negligible. The worked solution follows. The model. The soccer player is modeled as a particle moving horizontally in one dimension. We choose plus i hat to point forward in the direction of motion. The initial velocity is zero and the final velocity points in the plus i hat direction. Air resistance is negligible, so the average horizontal force exerted by the ground is the net horizontal force on the player. Vertical force is balance and do not affect the horizontal acceleration. The math. For one-dimensional horizontal motion, the average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time. A, first we determine the player's average acceleration. Since the player starts from rest and reaches a final velocity in the plus i hat direction, the change in velocity is change in vector v equals change in v i hat with change in v equals 8.00 meters per second. A equals change in v over change in t equals 8.00 meters per second over 2.50 seconds equals 3.20 meters per second squared. B, next we use Newton's second law to determine the average forward force exerted by the ground. Since air resistance is negligible, the forward ground force is the net horizontal force. Some fx equals max. Fnet equals ma. The average forward force follows from Newton's second law using the acceleration found in part A. Fnet equals 70.0 kilograms times 3.20 meters per second squared equals 224 Newton's. The conclusion. The soccer player's average acceleration is 3.20 meters per second squared in the forward direction. The average forward force exerted by the ground on the player is 224 Newton's. This force is reasonable because it is a moderate horizontal force applied over a short sprinting interval. Example problem. Force on a model helicopter. The problem. A 1.50 kilogram model helicopter has a velocity of 5.00 j hat meters per second at t equals 0. It is accelerated at a constant rate for 2.00 seconds after which it has a velocity of 6.00 i hat plus 12.00 j hat meters per second. What is the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the helicopter during this time interval? The work solution follows. The helicopter is modeled as a particle moving in two dimensions. We choose plus i hat to point horizontally and plus j hat to point vertically upward. The initial velocity points entirely in the plus j hat direction while the final velocity has both plus i hat and plus j hat components. The acceleration is constant over the time interval. The resultant force is the net external force responsible for this acceleration. The math. For constant acceleration, the acceleration vector is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time. The initial and final velocity vectors are V sub i equals 5.00 j hat meters per second. V sub f equals 6.00 i hat plus 12.00 j hat. The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity. The change in vector V equals vector V sub f minus vector V sub i equals 6.00 i hat meters per second plus 12.00 j hat meters per second minus 5.00 j hat meters per second equals 6.00 i hat plus 7.00 j hat meters per second. The acceleration follows from this change in velocity. Vector A equals change in vector V over change in T equals 6.00 i hat plus 7.00 j hat meters per second over 2.00 seconds equals 3.00 i hat plus 3.50 j hat meters per second squared. Newton's second law gives the resultant force vector. Some vector f equals M vector A equals 1.50 kilograms times 3.00 i hat plus 3.50 j hat meters per second squared. Equals 4.50 i hat plus 5.25 j hat Newton's. The magnitude of the resultant force is found from its components. F net equals square root of 4.50 Newton's squared plus 5.25 Newton's squared equals 6.91 Newton's. The conclusion. The resultant force acting on the model helicopter has magnitude 6.91 Newton's. The force points in the same direction as the acceleration vector with positive i hat and positive j hat components. Example problem. Baggage tractor. The problem. The figure on the course webpage shows a baggage tractor pulling luggage carts from an airplane. The tractor has mass 6.50 kilograms while cart A has mass 250 kilograms and cart B has mass 150 kilograms. The driving force acting for a brief period of time accelerates the system from rest and acts for 3 seconds. A. If this driving force is given by vector f equals 8.20 t i hat Newton's, find the speed after 3 seconds. B. What is the horizontal force acting on the connecting cable between the tractor and cart A at this instant? The worked solution follows. The model. The tractor and carts are modeled as particles moving together in one horizontal line. We choose plus i hat to point in the direction of motion. The driving force points in the plus i hat direction. The cable force on the tractor points in the minus i hat direction. While the cable force on cart A points in the plus i hat direction. Vertical forces balance and are not needed for the horizontal motion. The driving force varies with time so the acceleration also varies with time. The math for the full tractor cart system the driving force is the only external horizontal force. Newton's second law gives the acceleration of the entire system. Some f sub x equals m sub system A sub x. 820 t equals m sub t plus m sub A plus m sub B A. We solve this equation for the acceleration function. A of t equals 820 over m sub t plus m sub A plus m sub B t. A. First, we determine the speed after 3 seconds. Since A equals dv over dt and the system starts from rest the speed follows from integrating the acceleration. V equals the integral from 0 to 3.00 of 820 over 650 plus 250 plus 150 t dt. V equals 820 over 1050 times t squared over 2 evaluated from 0 to 3.00 equals 3.51 meters per second. B. Next, we isolate the tractor to find the cable force. At t equals 3.00 seconds the acceleration is A equals 820 over 1050 times 3.00 equals 2.34 meters per second squared. For the tractor alone the driving force points forward and the cable force points backward. Newton's second law gives 820 times 3.00 minus t equals m sub t A. t equals 820 times 3.00 minus 650 times 2.34. t equals 938 newtons. The conclusion. After 3 seconds the tractor and carts have speed 3.51 meters per second. At that instant the horizontal force in the cable between the tractor and cart A is 938 newtons. Treating the whole system gives the acceleration while isolating the tractor exposes the internal cable force. Bonus example problem. Projectal motion with quadratic drag. The problem. A 10 kilogram mortar shell is fired vertically upward from the ground with an initial velocity of 50 meters per second as shown in figure. Determine the maximum height it will travel if atmospheric resistance is measured as f sub d equals 0.01 v squared newtons where v is the speed at any instant. The worked solution follows. The model. The mortar shell is modeled as a particle moving vertically. We choose plus j hat to point upward and minus j hat to point downward. During the upward part of the motion the velocity points in the plus j hat direction so the drag force points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The drag magnitude depends on the instantaneous speed according to f sub d equals k v squared where k is the drag coefficient in this model. The shell reaches its maximum height when its upward speed becomes 0. The motion is 1 dimensional and g is treated as constant. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. Integral from 0 to h dy equals negative integral from v sub 0 to 0 v d v over g plus k over m v squared. h equals integral from 0 to v sub 0 v d v over g plus k over m v sub 0 squared. We evaluate the integral using the substitution u equals g plus k over m v squared so du equals 2 k over m v d v. This substitution changes the integral into the standard logarithmic form. h equals m over 2 k integral from g to g plus k over m v sub 0 squared du over u. h equals m over 2 k ln g plus k over m v sub 0 squared over g. The calculus note, why this integral becomes a logarithm? The integral has the form h equals integral from 0 to v sub 0 v d v over g plus k over m v squared. The denominator intains v squared while the numerator contains v d v. That pattern suggests defining a new variable using the denominator u equals g plus k over m v squared. Differentiating both sides gives du equals 2 k over m v d v. We solve this differential relation for v d v. v d v equals m over 2 k du. The original integral then becomes h equals integral v d v over g plus k over m v sub 0 squared equals integral m over 2 k du over u equals m over 2 k ln of u. Integral du over u equals natural log of absolute value of u plus c. For this problem, u is always positive because g plus k over m v squared is greater than 0. So the absolute value does not change the result. At the lower limit v equals 0 u equals g. At the upper limit v equals v sub 0 u equals g plus k over m v sub 0 to the power of 2. Therefore, h equals m over 2 k natural log of u evaluated from g to g plus k over m v sub 0 to the power of 2. We now evaluate the maximum height expression using the mass of the shell, the initial speed and the drag coefficient from the problem. h equals 10.00 kilograms over 2 times 0.0100 Newton second squared per square meters ln of 9.81 meters per second squared plus 0.00100 Newton second squared per square meter over 10.00 kilograms times 50.00 meters per second. h equals 9.81 meters per second squared plus 0.00100 Newton second squared over 9.81 meters per second squared equals 114 meters. The conclusion. The mortar shell reaches a maximum height of 114 meters. This height is lower than the no drag value because both the weight and the drag force point downward during the upward motion. The model predicts a variable acceleration because the drag force depends on speed.

segments.text: Application of Newton's Laws.
Solving Newton's Laws.
Note, this chapter combines several tools developed earlier in the course.
We use vector components from chapter 2, acceleration vectors from chapter 4,
and free body diagrams from chapter 5 to apply Newton's second law to real systems.
Problem-solving strategies.
Applying Newton's Laws of Motion.
Most problems in this chapter follow the same pattern.
Choose a system, identify the external forces, turn those forces into components,
and apply Newton's second law.
Define the system of interest.
Decide which object or group of objects you are analyzing.
Newton's second law uses only the external forces acting on that system.
Choose useful axes.
Pick coordinate axes that make the force components as simple as possible.
When motion occurs along a slope, curve, or rope, it is often useful to align one axis with the motion or acceleration.
Draw a free body diagram.
Draw only the external forces acting on the chosen system.
Do not draw velocity, acceleration, or the net force as separate forces.
Write Newton's second law by components.
Start from some vector f equals m vector a.
Then write the component equations such as some f sub x equals m a sub x,
and some f sub y equals m a sub y.
Use constraints and known conditions.
Constant velocity means a equals zero.
Static equilibrium means the net force is zero.
A massless rope has the same tension throughout.
A frictionless pulley changes the direction of the tension, but not its magnitude.
Solve symbolically before evaluating.
Keep the algebra general as long as possible.
Substitute numerical values only after the physical relationships are clear.
Check the result.
The answer should have the correct units, the correct direction, and a physically reasonable size.
This strategy is not a recipe for memorizing equations.
It is a way to translate a physical situation into Newton's second law.
The hardest step is usually deciding what belongs in the free body diagram and what does not.
See the flipping physics video on the course webpage.
Consider the challenge of lifting a grand piano into a second story apartment,
which of Newton's laws are involved.
Figure shows that we can represent all forces with arrows and simplify the analysis with a more crude representation.
It is important to make a list of knowns and unknowns so that we can properly identify the system of interest.
Recall that Newton's second law involves only external forces.
So we first list all the forces and then identify which are internal or external.
The identified forces are vector T, tension in the rope above the piano,
vector F sub T, force that the piano exerts on the rope, and vector W, weight of the piano.
All other forces, for example the nudge of a breeze, are assumed to be negligible.
Newton's third law can be used to identify whether forces are exerted between internal components of a system,
or between the system and an external component.
The vector T and vector F sub T form a force pair, where we only include the external component vector T in our free body diagram.
See Figure B.
Figure C shows a free body diagram where Newton's second law is applied in figure D.
Once external forces are clearly identified in free body diagrams, it should be straightforward to put them into Newton's second law and form equations that can be solved.
If the problem is one-dimensional, i.e. forces or parallel, then the forces can be handled algebraically.
If the problem is two-dimensional, then it must be broken into components and then solved as a pair of one-dimensional problems.
It is usually convenient to make one-axis parallel to the direction of motion, if this is known.
Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding.
Which forces act on the chosen system, and which forces act on something outside the system?
Then you have some F sub X equals M A sub X. Some F sub Y equals M A sub Y.
We must check the solution to tell whether it is reasonable. For example, it is reasonable to find that friction causes an object to slide down an incline more slowly than when no friction exists.
In practice, intuition, i.e. knowing what is reasonable at a glance, develops through solving many problems, i.e. experience.
Ut est rarem amniam magister usus. Experience is the teacher of all things, Julius Caesar.
Another way to check a solution is to check the units. If we are solving for force and end up with units of only velocity, then we have made a mistake.
Particle equilibrium. A particle in equilibrium is one that obeys Newton's first law, i.e. the external forces are balanced.
Static equilibrium involves objects at rest, and dynamic equilibrium involves objects in motion without acceleration.
Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. If an object is moving at constant velocity, is it an equilibrium?
What does that imply about the sum vector F?
Particle equilibrium is the force version of constant velocity. If the acceleration is zero, Newton's second law becomes sum vector F equals zero.
This extends the equilibrium ideas from Newton's first law and the free body diagram workflow from chapter 5.
Example problem. Different tensions at different angles. The problem. Consider the traffic light, mass of 15 kilograms,
suspended from two wires as shown in figure. Find the tension in each wire, neglecting the masses of the wires.
The worked solution follows. The model. The system of interest is the traffic light. We model the traffic light as a particle in static equilibrium, so its acceleration is zero.
We choose plus i hat to point horizontally to the right and plus j hat to point vertically upward.

With this coordinate choice, the left wire tension vector T sub 1 points up and to the left. The right wire tension vector T sub 2 points up and to the right, and the weight vector W points downward in the negative j hat direction.
The left wire makes an angle of 30 degrees with the horizontal, and the right wire makes an angle of 45 degrees with the horizontal.
The two wires are treated as massless and inexpensive, so each wire exerts a tension force along its own direction.
The only forces acting on the traffic light are the two tensions and the weight, similar to the tension in a tight rope.
Air resistance and motion of the light are neglected. The math. For static equilibrium, Newton's second law requires the net force on the traffic light to be zero.
Since the traffic light has no acceleration in either direction, some f sub x equals m a sub x equals zero. Some f sub y equals m a sub y equals zero.
The forces acting on the traffic light are the left tension vector T sub 1, the right tension vector T sub 2, and the weight vector W equals negative mg j hat.

Resolving the two tension forces into horizontal and vertical components gives the component equations. Some f sub x equals negative T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals zero.
Some f sub y equals T sub 1 sine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 sine 45 degrees minus mg equals zero.
The horizontal equation relates the two unknown tensions. We solve this equation for T sub 2 in terms of T sub 1 so that the vertical equation will contain only one unknown tension.
Negative T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals zero. T sub 2 cosine 45 degrees equals T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees.
The vertical equation determines the actual size of the tensions because the vertical components must balance the weight of the traffic light.
We substitute the horizontal equilibrium relation for T sub 2 into the vertical equation and solve for T sub 1.
T sub 1 sign 30 degrees plus T sub 2 sign 45 degrees minus mg equals 0.
T sub 1 sign 30 degrees plus T sub 2 cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sign 45 degrees equals mg.
T sub 1 times sign 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees sign 45 degrees equals mg.
T sub 1 equals mg over sine 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees
sine 45 degrees. The numerical value of T sub 1 follows from the vertical force balance,
and then the horizontal force balance gives T sub 2. T sub 1 equals 15.0 kilograms times
9.81 meters per second squared over sine 30 degrees plus cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees
sine 45 degrees equals 108 newtons. T sub 2 equals T sub 1 cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees
equals 108 newtons times cosine 30 degrees over cosine 45 degrees equals 132 newtons. The conclusion,
the tension in the left wire is T sub 1 equals 108 newtons, and the tension in the right wire is
T sub 2 equals 132 newtons. The right wire has the larger tension because its direction is closer
to vertical, so it supplies more of the upward force needed to balance the traffic light's weight.
These values satisfy newtons' second law for static equilibrium because the horizontal
components cancel and the vertical components balance the weight. Particle acceleration.
Instead of reducing the problem to a particle in static equilibrium where the sum of the net
forces equals 0, we can also reduce complex problems into one where the net force is non-zero,
or a particle with an acceleration. When the net force is not 0, the object accelerates in the
direction of the net force. The vector equation, the sum of the force vectors equals mass times
the acceleration vector, is solved component by component using the same vector component ideas
introduced in chapter 2. We'll look through four examples that illustrate different ways we can
decompose the complex motion into a simpler one. Drag force on a barge, net force in an elevator,
two attached blocks connected with a pulley, and at-wood machine vertical blocks with a pulley.
Note, it is useful to identify constraints that make a problem solvable. We saw this in the
tension in a tight-rope problem when identifying the tension. In chapter 5, we showed that the normal
force, a contact force, acts normal to the surface so that an object does not have an acceleration
perpendicular to the surface, meaning it stays static. The bathroom scale is an excellent example
of a normal force acting on a body. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding.
If the acceleration is 0 in one direction, but non-zero in another, which component equations of
Newton's second law still matter? A bathroom scale provides a measure of how much it must push
upward to support the weight of an object. The net force in an elevator problem will examine whether
we can predict what you would measure on a bathroom scale that is moving upward, either accelerating
or moving at constant speed. Do you think the scale will measure a different weight when the
elevator is moving at constant speed? What if the elevator is accelerating upward? Take a guess
before looking at the example problem. Example problem. Drag force on a barge. The problem.
Two tugboats push on a barge at different angles as shown in figure. The first tugboat exerts
a force of 2.7 times 10 to the fifth Newton's in the x direction, and the second tugboat exerts
a force of 3.6 times 10 to the fifth Newton's in the y direction. The mass of the barge is 5 times 10
to the sixth kilograms, and its acceleration is observed to be 7.5 times 10 to the minus 2 meters
per second squared in the direction shown. What is the drag force of the water on the barge
resisting the motion? Note. Drag force is a frictional force exerted by fluids such as air or water.
The drag force opposes the motion of the object. Since the barge is flat bottomed, we can assume
that the drag force is in the direction opposite the barge's motion. The worked solution follows.
The model. The system of interest is the barge. We model the barge as a rigid object
translating on the horizontal surface of the water. We choose plus i hat to point in the direction
of the first tugboats force, and plus j hat to point in the direction of the second tugboats force.
With this coordinate choice, the tugboat forces are vector f sub 1 equals f sub 1 i hat,
and vector f sub 2 equals f sub 2 j hat. The resultant tugboat force vector f sub
app points in the direction of the barge's observed acceleration. The drag force exerted by the
water points opposite the barge's motion, so it points opposite vector f sub app. The weight of
the barge and the buoyant force from the water balance vertically, so they are omitted from the
horizontal force model. The math. For horizontal motion, Newton's second law relates the net
horizontal force on the barge to the observed acceleration of the barge. The forces acting on
the barge in the horizontal plane are the tugboat forces vector f sub 1 and vector f sub 2,
and the drag force vector f sub d. The two tugboat forces combine to form the applied force vector
vector f sub app, and the drag force acts opposite the barge's motion. Newton's second law for
the horizontal motion is some vector f equals m vector a. Vector f sub app plus vector f sub d
equals m vector a. The two tugboat forces are perpendicular, so the magnitude and direction of
the applied force come from the vector components of vector f sub app. Resolving the applied force
into components gives vector f sub app equals f sub 1 i hat plus f sub 2 j hat.
f app equals square root of f sub 1 to the power of 2 plus f sub 2 to the power of 2.
Theta equals 10 to the power of minus 1 f sub 2 over f sub 1.
The applied force magnitude and direction follow from the perpendicular tugboat force components by
f app equals square root of 2.7 times 10 to the 5 newtons squared plus 3.6 times 10 to the 5 newtons squared
equals 4.5 times 10 to the 5 newtons. Theta equals 10 to the power of negative 1, 3.6 times 10 to the
5 over 2.7 times 10 to the 5 equals 53 degrees. Along the direction of motion the applied force
points forward and the drag force points backward. Newton's second law along this direction gives
f app minus f sub d equals ma. We solve this equation for the drag force magnitude which yields
f sub d equals f app minus ma. The drag force follows from Newton's second law along the direction
of motion as f sub d equals 4.5 times 10 to the 5 newtons minus 5 times 10 to the sixth
kilograms times 7.5 times 10 to the minus 2 meters per second squared equals 7.5 times 10 to the
4th newtons. The conclusion the water exerts a drag force with magnitude f sub d equals 7.5 times 10
to the 4th newtons. This drag force acts opposite the barge's motion while the tugboat resultant
points in the direction of motion. The result is consistent with Newton's second law because the
applied tugboat force is larger than the drag force leaving a net force that accelerates the barge.
Example problem, bathroom scale in an elevator. The problem, the figure on the course web page
shows a 75 kilogram man weight of about 165 pounds standing on a bathroom scale in an elevator.
Calculate the scale reading. A, if the elevator accelerates upward at a rate of 1.2 meters per second
squared, and B, if the elevator moves upward at a constant speed of 1 meter per second.
The worked solution follows. The model. The system of interest is the person standing on the scale.
We model the person as a particle moving vertically with the elevator. We choose plus j hat to point
upward and minus j hat to point downward. With this coordinate choice, the scale force on the
person points upward, so vector f sub s equals f sub s j hat, and the weight of the person points
downward, so vector w equals minus mg j hat. The scale reading is the magnitude of the upward
contact force f sub s. Air resistance is neglected, and the motion is one-dimensional along the vertical
axis. The math. For vertical motion, Newton's second law relates the net vertical force on the person
to the person's vertical acceleration. The forces acting on the person are the upward
scale force vector f sub s, and the downward weight vector w. Applying Newton's second law in
the vertical direction gives some f sub y equals m a sub y. f sub s minus mg equals m a sub y.
We solve this equation for the scale reading, f sub s, which yields f sub s equals mg plus m a sub y.
f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y. This equation shows that the scale reading depends on the
vertical acceleration of the person.
A. First, we evaluate the case when the elevator accelerates upward at a sub y equals 1.20 meters per
second squared. Since the acceleration points in the plus j hat direction, a sub y is positive.
f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y equals 75.0 kilograms times the quantity 9.81 meters per
second squared plus 1.20 meters per second squared equals 826 newtons. B. Then we evaluate the case
when the elevator moves upward at a constant speed of 1 meter per second. Constance speed implies
a sub y equals 0. So f sub s equals m times g plus a sub y equals 75.0 kilograms times 9.81 meters
per second squared plus 0 equals 736 newtons. The conclusion. When the elevator accelerates upward
at 1.20 meters per second squared, the scale reads f sub s equals 826 newtons. When the elevator
moves upward at constant speed, the acceleration is 0, and the scale reads f sub s equals 736 newtons.
The scale reading is larger during upward acceleration because the scale must exert enough
upward force to both balance the person's weight and produce the upward acceleration.
Example problem. Two attached blocks. The problem. The figure on the course web page shows a block
of mass m sub 1 on a frictionless horizontal surface. It is pulled by a light string that passes over
a frictionless and massless pulley. The other end of the string is connected to a block of mass m sub 2.
Find the acceleration of the blocks and the tension in the string in terms of m sub 1, m sub 2, and g.
The worked solution follows. The model. The system consists of two blocks connected by a light
inextensible string over a frictionless, massless pulley. Block m sub 1 moves horizontally on
a frictionless table and block m sub 2 moves vertically. The string constrains the blocks to have
the same acceleration magnitude. For block m sub 1, we choose plus i hat to point to the right
and plus j hat to point upward. With this convention, the tension vector t points in the plus i hat
direction. The normal force vector n points in the plus j hat direction and the weight vector w sub 1
points in the negative j hat direction. For block m sub 2, we use plus j hat upward,
so the tension vector t points in the plus j hat direction and the weight vector w sub 2 points
in the negative j hat direction. The hanging block accelerates downward while the block on the
table accelerates to the right. This example uses the same free body diagram workflow developed in
chapter 5. The important step here is to apply Newton's second law separately to each block
and then use the string constraint to relate their accelerations. The math. For the connected
block system, Newton's second law must be applied separately to each block because the tension
is an internal interaction between the two blocks. The forces acting on block m sub 1 are the
tension, the normal force, and its weight. The vertical forces on m sub 1 balance while the horizontal
tension provides its acceleration to the right. Applying Newton's second law to block m sub 1 gives
some f sub 1 x equals m sub 1 a t equals m sub 1 a. The forces acting on block m sub 2 are the
upward tension and the downward weight. Since plus j hat points upward, but m sub 2 accelerates
downward, its vertical acceleration is a sub 2 y equals minus a. Applying Newton's second law
to block m sub 2 gives some f sub 2 y equals m sub 2 a sub 2 y t minus m sub 2 g equals minus m sub
2 a. These two equations form the governing equations for the system t equals m sub 1 a t
minus m sub 2 g equals minus m sub 2 a. We solve these equations for the acceleration by substituting
t equals m sub 1 a into the equation for block m sub 2. m sub 1 a minus m sub 2 g equals minus
m sub 2 a m sub 1 a plus m sub 2 a equals m sub 2 g m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times a equals m sub 2 g
a equals m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g. We then use the block m sub 1 equation to solve
for the tension t equals m sub 1 a t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2
times g t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g. The conclusion,
the two blocks accelerate with magnitude a equals m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 times g.
Block m sub 1 accelerates to the right and block m sub 2 accelerates downward. The tension
in the string is t equals m sub 1 times m sub 2 over m sub 1 plus m sub 2 g. The acceleration
is less than g because the weight of the hanging block must accelerate both masses, not just m sub 2.
Example problem, at-wood machine. The problem, a classic problem in physics,
similar to the one we just solved, is the at-wood machine, which consists of a light rope running
over a frictionless pulley with two objects of different mass attached. It is particularly useful
in understanding the connection between force and motion. In figure, the masses are m sub 1
equals 2 kilograms and m sub 2 equals 4 kilograms. The pulley is frictionless. A, if m sub 2 is released,
what will its acceleration be? B, what is the tension in the string? The worked solution follows.
The model. Each mass is modeled as a particle connected by a light,
inextensible string over a frictionless, massless pulley. The ideal string and pulley
make the tension magnitude the same on both sides of the pulley. The string constraint makes
the blocks have the same acceleration magnitude. We choose plus j hat to point upward for both blocks.
With this convention, the tension on block m sub 1, points in the plus j hat direction
and the weight of block m sub 1 points in the minus j hat direction. The tension on block m sub 2
also points in the plus j hat direction and the weight of block m sub 2 points in the minus j
at direction. Since m sub 2 is greater than m sub 1, block m sub 2 accelerates downward
and block M sub 1 accelerates upward.
This problem is closely related to the previous attached blocks example.
In both problems, Newton's second law is applied separately to each block,
and the string constraint connects their accelerations.
The math.
For the at-wood machine, Newton's second law must be applied separately to each block,
because the tension is an internal interaction between the two masses.
The forces acting on block M sub 1 are the upward tension and the downward weight.
Since block M sub 1 accelerates upward in the plus j hat direction,
Newton's second law gives some F sub 1 y equals M sub 1 A.
T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A.
The forces acting on block M sub 2 are also the upward tension and the downward weight.
Since block M sub 2 accelerates downward while plus j hat points upward,
its acceleration is minus A j hat.
Newton's second law gives some F sub 2 y equals M sub 2 times minus A.
T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A.
These two equations form the governing equations for the system and will be reused in both parts.
T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A.
T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A.
A.
First, we determine the acceleration of the blocks after M sub 2 is released.
We eliminate the tension by subtracting the equation for block M sub 1 from the equation for block M sub 2
and then solve for A.
T minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 2 A minus M sub 1 A.
M sub 1 minus M sub 2 G equals minus M sub 1 plus M sub 2 A.
In turn, A equals M sub 2 minus M sub 1 over M sub 1 plus M sub 2 G.
The acceleration follows from the mass difference and the total mass being accelerated.
A equals 4.00 kilograms minus 2.00 kilograms over 4.00 kilograms plus 2.00 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared
equals 3.27 meters per second squared.
B.
Next, we find the tension in the string by reusing the equation for block M sub 1.
We solve that equation for T and substitute the acceleration found in part A.
T minus M sub 1 G equals M sub 1 A.
T equals M sub 1 times G plus A.
T equals 2.00 kilograms times 9.81 meters per second squared plus 3.27 meters per second squared
equals 26.2 newtons.
The conclusion.
The blocks accelerate with magnitude A equals 3.27 meters per second squared.
Block M sub 2 accelerates downward and block M sub 1 accelerates upward.
The tension in the string is T equals 26.2 newtons.
This result closely mirrors the attached blocks problem.
The acceleration is determined by the net unbalanced weight divided by the total mass being accelerated.
Newton's laws of motion and kinematics.
Newton's laws of motion can also be integrated with other concepts to solve problems of motion.
For example, forces produce accelerations, which was the main topic when discussing kinematics.
Newton's second law gives the acceleration.
Once the acceleration is known, the motion is found using the kinematics tools developed earlier,
including constant acceleration motion in chapter 3 and vector motion in chapter 4.
For problems that involve various types of forces, acceleration, velocity, or position,
it helps to identify the principles involved when listing the givens and quantities to be calculated.
The following examples illustrate how to apply the problem solving strategies.
These example problems are soccer player at top speed, force on a model helicopter,
force on a baggage tractor, and the motion of a vertical projectile as a bonus.
Checkpoint.
Pause and check your understanding.
When a force determines acceleration first, which kinematics quantities should you compute next,
velocity, position, or time?
Recall that V equals DS over DT and A equals DV over DT.
This means that we can use the calculus forms when acceleration is not constant,
meaning A equals a function of S, V, and T.
First, we solve for DT in each equation, then set them equal to each other.
DT equals DS divided by V, DT equals DV divided by A.
So, A DS equals V DV.
When A is a function of V, we can apply the following integrals.
A of V times the integral of DS equals the integral of V DV,
and the integral of DS equals the integral of V divided by A of V with respect to V.
Example problem.
Soccer player top speed.
The problem.
A soccer player starts at rest and accelerates forward reaching a velocity of 8 meters per second in 2.5 seconds.
A, what is her average acceleration?
B, what average force does the ground exert forward on the runner so that she achieves this acceleration?
The player's mass is 70 kilograms and air resistance is negligible.
The worked solution follows.
The model.
The soccer player is modeled as a particle moving horizontally in one dimension.
We choose plus i hat to point forward in the direction of motion.
The initial velocity is zero and the final velocity points in the plus i hat direction.
Air resistance is negligible, so the average horizontal force exerted by the ground is the net horizontal force on the player.
Vertical force is balance and do not affect the horizontal acceleration.
The math.
For one-dimensional horizontal motion, the average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time.
A, first we determine the player's average acceleration.
Since the player starts from rest and reaches a final velocity in the plus i hat direction, the change in velocity is
change in vector v equals change in v i hat with change in v equals 8.00 meters per second.
A equals change in v over change in t equals 8.00 meters per second over 2.50 seconds equals 3.20 meters per second squared.
B, next we use Newton's second law to determine the average forward force exerted by the ground.
Since air resistance is negligible, the forward ground force is the net horizontal force.
Some fx equals max.
Fnet equals ma.
The average forward force follows from Newton's second law using the acceleration found in part A.
Fnet equals 70.0 kilograms times 3.20 meters per second squared equals 224 Newton's.
The conclusion. The soccer player's average acceleration is 3.20 meters per second squared in the forward direction.
The average forward force exerted by the ground on the player is 224 Newton's.
This force is reasonable because it is a moderate horizontal force applied over a short sprinting interval.
Example problem. Force on a model helicopter.
The problem. A 1.50 kilogram model helicopter has a velocity of 5.00 j hat meters per second at t equals 0.
It is accelerated at a constant rate for 2.00 seconds after which it has a velocity of 6.00 i hat plus 12.00 j hat meters per second.
What is the magnitude of the resultant force acting on the helicopter during this time interval?
The work solution follows.
The helicopter is modeled as a particle moving in two dimensions.
We choose plus i hat to point horizontally and plus j hat to point vertically upward.
The initial velocity points entirely in the plus j hat direction while the final velocity has both plus i hat and plus j hat components.
The acceleration is constant over the time interval.
The resultant force is the net external force responsible for this acceleration.
The math. For constant acceleration, the acceleration vector is the change in velocity divided by the elapsed time.
The initial and final velocity vectors are V sub i equals 5.00 j hat meters per second.
V sub f equals 6.00 i hat plus 12.00 j hat.
The change in velocity is the final velocity minus the initial velocity.

The change in vector V equals vector V sub f minus vector V sub i equals 6.00 i hat meters per second plus 12.00 j hat meters per second minus 5.00 j hat meters per second equals 6.00 i hat plus 7.00 j hat meters per second.

The acceleration follows from this change in velocity. Vector A equals change in vector V over change in T equals 6.00 i hat plus 7.00 j hat meters per second over 2.00 seconds equals 3.00 i hat plus 3.50 j hat meters per second squared.
Newton's second law gives the resultant force vector. Some vector f equals M vector A equals 1.50 kilograms times 3.00 i hat plus 3.50 j hat meters per second squared.
Equals 4.50 i hat plus 5.25 j hat Newton's. The magnitude of the resultant force is found from its components.
F net equals square root of 4.50 Newton's squared plus 5.25 Newton's squared equals 6.91 Newton's.

The conclusion. The resultant force acting on the model helicopter has magnitude 6.91 Newton's. The force points in the same direction as the acceleration vector with positive i hat and positive j hat components.
Example problem. Baggage tractor. The problem. The figure on the course webpage shows a baggage tractor pulling luggage carts from an airplane.
The tractor has mass 6.50 kilograms while cart A has mass 250 kilograms and cart B has mass 150 kilograms.
The driving force acting for a brief period of time accelerates the system from rest and acts for 3 seconds.
A. If this driving force is given by vector f equals 8.20 t i hat Newton's, find the speed after 3 seconds.
B. What is the horizontal force acting on the connecting cable between the tractor and cart A at this instant? The worked solution follows.
The model. The tractor and carts are modeled as particles moving together in one horizontal line. We choose plus i hat to point in the direction of motion.
The driving force points in the plus i hat direction. The cable force on the tractor points in the minus i hat direction.
While the cable force on cart A points in the plus i hat direction. Vertical forces balance and are not needed for the horizontal motion.
The driving force varies with time so the acceleration also varies with time. The math for the full tractor cart system the driving force is the only external horizontal force.
Newton's second law gives the acceleration of the entire system. Some f sub x equals m sub system A sub x.
820 t equals m sub t plus m sub A plus m sub B A. We solve this equation for the acceleration function.
A of t equals 820 over m sub t plus m sub A plus m sub B t.
A. First, we determine the speed after 3 seconds. Since A equals dv over dt and the system starts from rest the speed follows from integrating the acceleration.
V equals the integral from 0 to 3.00 of 820 over 650 plus 250 plus 150 t dt.
V equals 820 over 1050 times t squared over 2 evaluated from 0 to 3.00 equals 3.51 meters per second.
B. Next, we isolate the tractor to find the cable force. At t equals 3.00 seconds the acceleration is A equals 820 over 1050 times 3.00 equals 2.34 meters per second squared.
For the tractor alone the driving force points forward and the cable force points backward. Newton's second law gives 820 times 3.00 minus t equals m sub t A.
t equals 820 times 3.00 minus 650 times 2.34. t equals 938 newtons. The conclusion. After 3 seconds the tractor and carts have speed 3.51 meters per second.
At that instant the horizontal force in the cable between the tractor and cart A is 938 newtons.
Treating the whole system gives the acceleration while isolating the tractor exposes the internal cable force.

Bonus example problem. Projectal motion with quadratic drag. The problem. A 10 kilogram mortar shell is fired vertically upward from the ground with an initial velocity of 50 meters per second as shown in figure.
Determine the maximum height it will travel if atmospheric resistance is measured as f sub d equals 0.01 v squared newtons where v is the speed at any instant.
The worked solution follows. The model. The mortar shell is modeled as a particle moving vertically. We choose plus j hat to point upward and minus j hat to point downward.
During the upward part of the motion the velocity points in the plus j hat direction so the drag force points downward in the minus j hat direction.

The weight also points downward in the minus j hat direction. The drag magnitude depends on the instantaneous speed according to f sub d equals k v squared where k is the drag coefficient in this model.
The shell reaches its maximum height when its upward speed becomes 0. The motion is 1 dimensional and g is treated as constant.

The calculus note, why this integral becomes a logarithm? The integral has the form h equals integral from 0 to v sub 0 v d v over g plus k over m v squared.
The denominator intains v squared while the numerator contains v d v. That pattern suggests defining a new variable using the denominator u equals g plus k over m v squared.
Differentiating both sides gives du equals 2 k over m v d v.
We solve this differential relation for v d v. v d v equals m over 2 k du.
The original integral then becomes h equals integral v d v over g plus k over m v sub 0 squared equals integral m over 2 k du over u equals m over 2 k ln of u.
Integral du over u equals natural log of absolute value of u plus c. For this problem, u is always positive because g plus k over m v squared is greater than 0.
So the absolute value does not change the result.
At the lower limit v equals 0 u equals g. At the upper limit v equals v sub 0 u equals g plus k over m v sub 0 to the power of 2.
Therefore, h equals m over 2 k natural log of u evaluated from g to g plus k over m v sub 0 to the power of 2.

The conclusion. The mortar shell reaches a maximum height of 114 meters. This height is lower than the no drag value because both the weight and the drag force point downward during the upward motion.
The model predicts a variable acceleration because the drag force depends on speed.
